0.27.0.lead: Anyone already running a media server already has the people. This release brings them across: Nexview asks Plex, Jellyfin or Emby for its accounts, you tick whoever you want, and those people then sign in with the credentials they already use. No invitation, no password, no e-mail address.

sections.title: Take over existing accounts from the media server
sections.where: Settings, Services, Media server, open a tile, Existing accounts
sections.body: Until now an account came into being only when somebody signed in for the first time. With Jellyfin and Emby none came into being at all: neither knows an e-mail address for an account, and without one Nexview cannot tell a new person from somebody who has had an account for years. For thirty people that meant creating thirty accounts by hand, setting thirty passwords and passing them on. Now Nexview shows the server's accounts as a list, you tick them, and for each row you decide: a new account, or link it to one that already exists. Nothing is preselected, and linking is never the default.

sections.title: Newly created accounts can be given their limits right away
sections.where: Same window, at the bottom, For newly created accounts
sections.body: Movies, shows and storage, each as house default, unlimited or a fixed number. Plus a tick that creates the accounts inactive, in case you want to enable them later. An account that is merely linked keeps its own limits untouched: they were set deliberately once, and an import that overwrites them in passing would take them away without saying so anywhere. The role is not on offer, it is always a plain user, and requests need approval.

sections.title: Whoever was taken over signs in with the media server
sections.where: Sign-in page, sign in with Plex, Jellyfin or Emby
sections.body: The import creates the account and the link in one step, and the link is the actual work: without it there would be an account nobody can get into. That is why the new accounts get no password and no e-mail address. Give one a password anyway and that person has to add an address first, or the address confirmation stops them. The window says so.

sections.title: The block list is now there for all three servers
sections.where: Settings, Services, Media server, Blocked accounts
sections.body: When an account is deleted, its media-server identity lands on a block list so that it cannot simply create itself again at the next sign-in. That list used to be visible for Plex only, because with Jellyfin and Emby no account could come into being anyway. With the import that is no longer true, so it is there everywhere now. If somebody you want to take over is on it, the row says so, and Nexview asks once before lifting the block.

small: The watcher over the owner account now reads the whole backend instead of the routers alone. A write to a foreign account moved out into a service used to slip past it.

The field names it recognises a foreign account by now come from the database's foreign keys instead of a hand-written list. Four of the seven old names existed nowhere in the schema; eight real ones were missing.

secret.key is now created with mode 0600 instead of 0644, and existing installations are tightened too. The backups inside the data directory are unencrypted, and the README and the interface now say so.
A watcher over the age filter measures at runtime whether a blocked title comes out anywhere.
The schema fingerprint makes a renamed column visible in the diff, and the start now names columns the database still has and the model does not.

0.26.2.lead: Under the hood. This release brings no new feature, and that is deliberate: it repairs a setting that turned itself around behind your back, makes the lists a lot faster, and clears out what had piled up out of sight. There is almost nothing to see. There is something to notice.

sections.title: A storage limit of 0 turned into its opposite on every restart
sections.where: Settings, Users, the storage limit column
sections.body: Giving an account 0 GB meant: this account may not request anything. On the next start Nexview turned that into unlimited, the exact opposite, and said nothing about it. The cause was a migration step from version 0.19 that kept running on every start instead of once. It is fixed, and not only for that one step: Nexview now keeps a book of which migrations have run, and that book survives an update that breaks off halfway. What already flipped in the past cannot be recovered; a rewritten 0 looks exactly like a deliberate unlimited in the database. If your installation is affected, a note appears in the log on the next start.

sections.title: Lists fetch their data in one go
sections.where: Requests, user management, dashboard
sections.body: The pending requests list asked the database once per row for that row's rating: 157 small questions for 144 rows, and more the longer the list got. It is eleven now. Same for the user list and the dashboard. What is displayed is exactly what was displayed before, checked character by character. To keep it that way, the test run no longer measures whether the number is small but whether it grows when the data doubles.

sections.title: The database gives deleted space back by itself
sections.where: Nothing to do, happens at startup and then in the background
sections.body: Expired cache entries were deleted, but their space stayed in the file, so it only ever grew: 172 MB of file for 32 MB of content, measured. Nexview converts the database once on the first start of this version and reclaims the space gradually after that. On the measured database that was 180 MB before and 34 MB after. The first start takes a little longer because of it, once, and says so in the log.

sections.title: Four libraries raised to a safe version
sections.where: Nothing to do, it is in the image
sections.body: Nexview gets by with eleven third-party libraries where comparable applications need seventy-seven. Four of them sat on versions with published advisories, including the ones responsible for sign-in and encryption. All four are raised. From now on a check holds the pinned versions against the public vulnerability database on every build, and stops the build instead of merely warning.

small: **The interface loads less.** The texts in this window used to travel along with every page load, although only an operator reads them and only once after an update. They arrive on demand now. The first load drops from 822 to 792 kB.

**The badge on the admin menu goes away again.** It counted findings, and a finding stays true as long as it is true, so the same digit sat there forever even after somebody had looked. It counts unread now.

**Backups and maintenance no longer get in each other's way.** The hourly beat and restoring a backup could block one another. They take turns now, and restoring leaves the interface reachable while it runs.

**The workshop was tidied up.** Two checkers now watch the Python side and the interface, and the build on GitHub takes seven minutes instead of forty. Nobody notices that but me, and it makes every future repair faster.

0.26.1.lead: A maintenance release: no new feature, seven repairs. Two of them turned up while trying the others out, and one had left a series behind in a real Sonarr that had no business being there.

sections.title: Descriptions that existed but nobody saw
sections.where: Everywhere titles appear: catalogue, title page, season view
sections.body:
“No description available.” often stood where TMDB does have a plot, just not in your language. TMDB keeps the text separately per language and does not fall back on its own; where the translation is missing, the answer carries an empty text rather than the original.

Nexview now fetches the English one, for titles as well as seasons and episodes. Measured against a real library: 64 of 454 titles carried no description, 29 of them from this year, which is exactly what the catalogue puts at the front.

sections.title: Series that could not be requested
sections.where: When requesting a series
sections.body:
Sonarr adds series by their TVDB id, and that came from TMDB alone. For new titles TMDB regularly does not have it, and the request failed with a sentence that sounded like “wait a few days” and often was not the case at all.

Nexview now also asks Sonarr, which knows the same series through its own search. Where a hit carries the same TMDB number, the match is certain and nothing is asked. Otherwise the suggestions are put up, with what you actually requested right beside them. Because “Still Water” (Thailand, 2026) and “Still Waters” (Wales, 1995) are one letter apart and two different shows; no guessing happens here.

Where none of them fit, the line underneath says whether waiting helps, and it says something different for a series from last week than for one from 1978.

sections.title: Future seasons now count against your storage quota
sections.where: When requesting a series, the “also future seasons” tick box
sections.body:
The tick box is a promise: keep this series coming. The storage accounting read that inconsistently. Somebody who requested a whole series was charged for later seasons, somebody who requested season 1 and ticked the box was not. The same wish, two answers.

Both answer the same way now. The **count** quota counts wishes: a season appearing later costs no further slot, because at request time nobody can say how many there will be. The **storage** quota counts gigabytes, and those exist once the season is downloaded, so they land on whoever ticked the box.

This applies to seasons arriving from now on. What has already been attributed stays where it is.

sections.title: “Cancel” now says what it actually does
sections.where: My requests, and Settings → All requests
sections.body:
The confirmation always announced that the title would be removed from Radarr or Sonarr, that the quota would be freed, and that downloaded files would be deleted with it. For a **failed** request none of that is true: it never got as far as being added, and it costs no quota either.

Reported by an operator who found series in that list which he had long since downloaded, with a warning pointing at their files. It now says what really happens, and the warning only appears when there is something to delete.

small: **A failed request no longer leaves anything behind.** Adding a series and switching its season on are two steps; when the second failed, the series stood in Sonarr without a season and without a file. What the failed attempt created is taken back now, only that, and without deleting files.

**“No seasons yet” does not mean “does not have that season”.** Sonarr loads the data of a freshly added series in the background. Asking straight afterwards returned a series without seasons and therefore a refusal. Nexview waits for it now; the sync switches the season on in its next pass.

**The log is English throughout again.** Five lines wrote the German sentence of an error into it, and a warning in the Sonarr part would have crashed instead of warning. A new guard finds such lines at build time.

0.26.0.lead: Until now all administrators were equal. Appointing a second one also handed them the power to throw out the first. From this version on, exactly one account carries the **owner** flag — and it is the one account nobody else can switch off.

sections.title: One account nobody else can touch
sections.where: Settings → Users — look for the “Owner” badge
sections.body:
Whoever set the application up, pays for the electricity and holds the hard disk in their hands — and was still as removable as anyone else. There was exactly one brake against that, and it applied too late: only the *last* active administrator was protected. As long as a second one was around, anyone could remove anyone.

Now exactly one account carries the flag. When another administrator opens it in the user list, the buttons are **greyed out** — switch off, demote, delete, change quotas, set the password — with a sentence next to them explaining why. Not clickable followed by an error: not clickable in the first place.

**The worst of the five doors was the password.** Until now it had no brake at all, not even the one for the last administrator. A second administrator did not have to throw the first one out: they set a password and **became** them — with their access keys, their child accounts, their way in. The log held one inconspicuous line.

⚠️ **The flag grants no rights whatsoever.** No automatic approval, no larger quota, no power over anyone else's access keys. It says only what **others** may not do with this account. Whoever runs the installation therefore sees no difference in their own interface — apart from the badge and one new section in their profile.

sections.title: Handing it on — once, and with no way back
sections.where: Profile → Security → “Hand over ownership”
sections.body:
Only the holder can hand the flag on. There is no way to take it. In their profile they pick another administrator, read a warning that says what applies afterwards, and confirm.

Afterwards they are an ordinary administrator — the new owner, and every other administrator, can switch off, demote and delete their account and set their password. They cannot take the flag back; only the new holder can hand it back.

Handing over works only to an **active administrator**. Not to an ordinary account, not to an approver, not to a child account, not to a disabled account and not to yourself — otherwise the flag would sit on an account that could never pass it on.

While someone carries the flag, they cannot close their own account: hand it on first, then leave.

sections.title: The way back if you lock yourself out
sections.where: docker-compose.yml — for emergencies only, nowhere else
sections.body:
Password forgotten with no mail delivery set up, login provider dead, account accidentally unusable: the flag would never move again. That is what the emergency hammer is for. Add `NEXVIEW_BETREIBER=yourusername` and restart the container — that account carries the flag afterwards, with one line in the log. Then take the line out again.

On a new installation you need to know none of this: the account from the setup wizard gets the flag by itself. If the variable names an account that does not exist, **nothing** happens beyond a warning in the log — a typo does not create an account.

If the line stays in place, the owner is permanently fixed from outside. Handing over in the profile is then explicitly **refused**, with a reason, rather than silently springing back on the next restart.

⚠️ **And the boundary that comes with it:** the flag protects against a second administrator, not against someone with access to your server. Whoever can restart the container already has full control over Nexview and its database.

sections.title: Two side doors, also closed
sections.where: Settings → Media server and login providers, and Backups
sections.body:
The owner can also be dealt with without ever touching their account — and both routes are closed too.

**Switching off their way in.** Anyone who only gets in through a login provider or the media server is left outside as soon as it is gone. Their account is untouched and unreachable. Until now an administrator could override that warning; for the owner they no longer can. For every other account overriding stays allowed — there the administrator can repair the damage afterwards by setting a password. For the owner that is exactly what they may not do.

**Restoring an old backup.** It copies the whole database, so the flag would have travelled with it — and a handover could be undone that way. The owner flag is therefore the one value that does not join the time machine: after a restore it is carried by whoever carried it before. If that account does not exist in the backup, it stays unassigned rather than being guessed.

sections.title: House rules: your own text, if you want one
sections.where: Settings → House rules
sections.body: What may be requested, how long titles stay, who to write to when something is broken: you can write it down now instead of explaining it once in a message nobody finds again. Anyone signed in reaches it through a **§ button in the bottom right corner**. **Entirely optional** — leave the field empty and there is no button either.

small: Existing installations: after the update the **oldest active administrator** gets the flag — usually the account from the setup wizard. If there is no active administrator, it stays visibly unassigned instead of quietly appointing someone.
The database itself enforces that there can never be two owners — not just the program code.
A new check walks the **entire** list of endpoints on every build and fails as soon as someone adds one that can change another account without having decided about owner protection.

0.25.1.lead: A maintenance release — nothing new to discover, but a lot that is now correct. Two **security holes** are closed, the **library sync** no longer gives up on a slow media server, and **sixteen error messages** used to arrive in German whatever language you had chosen.

sections.title: Two security holes
sections.where: Affects every installation — nothing to set up
sections.body:
**Passwords could be guessed.** The sign-in brake named three doors where a password is checked. There was a fourth: resending the confirmation mail and correcting an unconfirmed address. Measured: a hundred wrong passwords, a hundred refusals, not once slowed down — and the answer told the caller when a guess was right. Anyone able to reach Nexview from the network could try passwords for every account, yours included, without holding one of their own.

**Access keys survived “sign out everywhere”.** They take a second path through the sign-in that never asked whether the session was still valid. Somebody whose laptop was stolen locked the thief out of sessions but not out of keys. “Sign out everywhere” now revokes them and says so beforehand; a routine password change leaves them alone and points at where to revoke them.

sections.title: The library sync no longer gives up
sections.where: Settings → Media servers → Library sync
sections.body:
Every request to a media server had fifteen seconds, whatever it asked for. A library big enough — or a server slow enough — missed that limit. And because one missed chunk takes the entire run with it, the card did not read “half done” afterwards, it read “Not synced yet.”

The time limit is no longer a fixed number. Nexview now asks in chunks whose size **the server decides**: a chunk that misses its time is halved and the same place asked again, and what gets through is kept for the rest of the run. A library twice the size needs twice as many chunks, but each one fits. There is nothing to configure.

It was reported for Jellyfin while Emby on the same installation kept working. Both run through the same code — the Jellyfin server was simply the slower of the two.

sections.title: Error messages in your language
sections.where: Everywhere something goes wrong
sections.body:
Sixteen messages arrived in German whatever language was set — among them the very first contact with Nexview, an expired invitation link. All of them are named now, so the interface can say them in your language.

Media-server timeouts joined them in this release: anyone working in English used to read “Der Jellyfin-Server antwortet nicht”.

sections.title: What the interface claimed that was not true
sections.where: My requests, Liked, a child's wishes
sections.body:
Three pages showed their empty text when loading had **failed**. Somebody with twelve running requests read “you have not requested anything yet”.

An approver was told about new feedback by the bell, followed it, and read “there is no unanswered feedback” — the address behind it required an administrator. Approvers may read now; answering is still not theirs.

And a crash while drawing wiped the whole interface, navigation included. The likeliest trigger is an update with a tab left open. There is a net there now, with one visible way out.

small: A silent Radarr deleted the whole storage accounting: no answer meant no titles, and everything the instance would have reported counted as gone. Because the rows were deleted, deletion deadlines and releases were lost for good. The rule from the status sync now holds here too: **not answering is not a no.**
Cleaning up several quality profiles at once forgot the ownership record for all of them — including the ones the instance refused to delete. Those stayed in Radarr but counted as foreign here.
The bell sent two kinds of notification to the wrong page. Where a click leads was answered in two places that disagreed; there is one list now, and it covers all 26 kinds.
The heart and the bin swallowed every failed click. They report it themselves now, where the eye already is — and a screen reader says it too.
A child was shown TMDB's technical text. The reason goes to the log instead.
A link to a conditional settings sub-tab always landed on “General”. Only the conditional ones were affected — which is why anyone testing a working one called the link healthy.
“Library touched” read “0 %” above “2 of 0 titles”. Without a stock the share is not zero, it is unknown — a dash says that now.
The health check in docker-compose.yml ignored NEXVIEW_PORT: following our own instructions produced a container that runs and still counts as unhealthy.

0.25.0.lead: This release turns Nexview into a **tool for whoever runs it**. There is a dedicated **admin dashboard** that tells you within ten seconds whether something is broken. “Statistics” becomes **Statistics & analysis** with six tabs — right down to **who is watching what right now** and whether your server is transcoding for it. And you can now **sign in through Authentik, Keycloak, Pocket ID or Google**.

sections.title: Sign in through an external provider
sections.where: Settings → System → Sign-in
sections.body:
Nexview can hang off a sign-in service you already run — **Authentik, Keycloak, Pocket ID, Google** or anything else that speaks OpenID Connect. A button per provider then appears on the sign-in page.

An existing account can be linked from your profile; new people can be created automatically if you want, with the role and quota you set. Your password keeps working — the external provider is added, it replaces nothing.

Setup guides for the four common services are in the README.

sections.title: The admin dashboard
sections.where: Button on the home page, or the menu under your name
sections.body:
Until now everything operational was spread across thirty settings pages. Now there is **one place** that says: three requests awaiting approval, Sonarr has not answered for two hours, the disk is 94 percent full.

Twenty checks run in the background. Every **finding** says not only what is, but **what follows from it** — and the button next to it takes you exactly where you fix it. Not to “Settings”, but to *Settings → Services → Sonarr*.

The most valuable check is the quietest one: **requests that have been searching for over two weeks.** In the interface “searching” looks like work, not like a standstill — until now it only surfaced when somebody complained.

sections.title: Statistics & analysis
sections.where: Menu under your name → Statistics & analysis
sections.body:
One page of numbers becomes **six tabs**: requests, people, watching, library, services, operations. Each opens with the findings for its area and backs them up with figures.

New under **library**: source reconciliation. Radarr manages the files, the media server plays them, Nexview bills them to somebody — and where the three disagree, errors appear that nobody looks for, because nothing is red anywhere. Titles with no identifier, year conflicts, files the media server never scanned in.

⚠️ The page is now **for administrators only**. Approvers could see it before; it now carries instance state, disk usage and backups.

sections.title: Who is watching — and whether the server is sweating
sections.where: Statistics & analysis → Watching
sections.body:
Nexview now shows **live playback** across every connected media server: who, what, on which device, how far in — and how hard your server is working for it.

There are **three** states here, not two. “Transcoding” sounds like yes or no, and it is not: both Plex and Emby report a transcode while passing the video through untouched and only re-encoding the audio — which costs almost nothing. **Only video transcoding is red**, the one that actually eats CPU. Along with why it is transcoding and whether your GPU is helping.

Below that: how much gets watched and by whom, how the library grew, and how many streams ran at the same time.

sections.title: A tile for your home dashboard
sections.where: Profile → Account → Security (token), guide in docs/dashboard-tile.md
sections.body:
If you use Homepage, Homarr or a similar board as your start page, Nexview can now sit on it with real numbers: open approvals, findings, library size, instance state — **one call**, with ready-made config snippets to copy.

The address lives under `/api/v1`, which makes it a promise: what is in it today will not disappear again.

small: Links land where the thing actually is: *Settings → Services → Sonarr* instead of just “Settings”, and *Requests → Failed* instead of the full list.
The requests tab now shows how long your people typically wait for an approval — and how long the oldest open one has been sitting there.

The disk ring separates **media**, **everything else** and **free**. “Used versus free” would be a half-truth: backups, photos and the operating system live on the same disk, and only “media” can be cleaned up through Nexview.
Nexview remembers since when an instance stopped answering. “Restarting right now” and “gone since last night” are two different messages.

0.24.0.lead: Three things in this release. Nexview now fits behind a reverse proxy under a **sub-path** — `yourdomain.com/nexview` instead of its own subdomain. The **profile store can travel**: save it as a file, read it in elsewhere, and Nexview recognises its own copies. And Nexview warns when **two instances share one download category** — the mistake that looks like a network fault.

sections.title: A sub-path behind the reverse proxy
sections.where: docker-compose → NEXVIEW_URL_BASE, examples in the README
sections.body:
One line in your docker-compose — `NEXVIEW_URL_BASE=/nexview` —, restart the container, and Nexview lives at `https://yourdomain.com/nexview/`. Both common proxy styles work: **passing the path through and stripping it**, whichever guide your proxy was set up from.

Sign-in, images, downloads and the API docs all follow the prefix. If you set nothing, nothing changes — without the variable everything stays exactly as before. Copy-paste examples for nginx, Caddy, Traefik and Nginx Proxy Manager are in the README.

sections.title: The public address thinks along
sections.where: Settings → Addresses
sections.body: The public address goes into every link Nexview sends. With a sub-path set, Nexview now suggests it **with the prefix included** — and warns when a hand-typed address is missing it. Before, invitations and password links would have led nowhere, silently.

sections.title: The profile store can travel
sections.where: Settings → Services → Quality profiles → “Save the store” / “Read a store”
sections.body:
Set up Nexview fresh and point it at the same Radarr, and until now it stood before its **own** profiles as before strangers — which number belongs to whom lives only in Nexview's database. Now the store can be saved as a file and read back in elsewhere: Nexview recognises its copies on the instances by name and adopts them, id included.

A preview shows what would happen before anything is read in; nothing is written to Radarr or Sonarr in the process. The file holds recipes and names only — no credentials — which also makes it the way to hand a profile to somebody else.

sections.title: Two instances, one category — now warned about
sections.where: Settings → Services
sections.body:
When two Radarr or Sonarr instances share one category in the download client, each grabs the other's downloads: requests sit on “downloading”, files land in the wrong library — and no error appears anywhere. So people go looking at the network or the indexer. Radarr cannot warn about it, it does not know the second instance exists — Nexview does, and now warns, including when an instance runs without a category of its own.

The category itself has to be created in the download client; Radarr and Sonarr cannot do that. If you share on purpose, click “This is intended” — should a third instance later land on the same category, the warning returns.

small: A permanent browser test now checks sub-path operation automatically with every release — in both proxy styles.

0.28.0.lead: Until now the account setting decided every request. This version puts a list in front of it: “wave through documentaries rated 5 and up”, “don't even start with films below 5”. Nexview walks the list from top to bottom and takes the first rule that matches. If none does, everything stays as before.

sections.title: Rules that decide requests
sections.where: Settings, Rules
sections.body: A rule is a set of conditions that all have to hold, and one consequence: approve at once, or decline. Conditions can use the type, the genre, the rating, the number of votes, the release year, the runtime, the original language, the age rating, the requested tier and what is already here. If you need an “or”, add a second rule - that keeps the list readable and is the very reason Nexview can work out contradictions at all. Where one rule overtakes another, the list says so and offers a click to reorder.

sections.title: Book to house stock
sections.where: Settings, Rules, add a rule, under “approve at once”
sections.body: If you want well-rated new releases to be there at once without burdening anybody, tick this: the title then counts against nobody's storage quota. The item count still applies - that hangs on the request, not on the storage entry, and it renews every week anyway.

sections.title: What a rule cannot do
sections.where: Settings, Rules, in the box at the top
sections.body: Three things stay out of reach, and none of them is a matter of ordering. The age filter acts when listing: what an account cannot see, it cannot request. A child's wish always goes to the parents. And the requester's quota is checked before the rules and wins - even against a rule that would have booked the title to house stock. Rules do not apply to administrators and approvers at all, just like the block list.

sections.title: Declined does not mean vanished
sections.where: My requests
sections.body: Where a rule declines, the request is still created - in the declined state, with the reason you wrote into the rule, and with the rule's name in the history. The requester is notified the same way a decision by hand would notify them. Per rule you can allow them to send it to an approver anyway; the approver then sees a badge saying a rule had declined it.

small: A rule matching on genre now compares numbers rather than names. Names are translated - the same documentary is called something else in each language, and the rule would have worked in one and not the other.
TMDB reports a rating of 0.0 with zero votes, indistinguishable from a real zero. “Rating below 5, decline” would have caught every unrated title - and unrated mostly means new.
The same for a series runtime: for some, TMDB reports zero minutes, and that means “we don't know”.
“View single titles” under your storage led to the profile menu instead of the storage tab. The clean-up mail pointed at a tab name that does not exist.

0.29.0.lead: Whoever runs Seerr and wants to switch used to start from nothing: every account by hand, every quota a second time, Radarr and Sonarr typed in once more. This version reads a running Seerr during first-time setup and takes over everything that has a place in Nexview.

sections.title: A third way into setup: from a running Seerr
sections.where: On the very first start, front page of the wizard
sections.body: Nexview reads Seerr through its API with the key you paste, shows what it found area by area, and writes only what you tick: Radarr and Sonarr with their keys and folders, the mail server including its password, region and language, the house quota default, the block list, and the notification channels for Discord, Telegram, Gotify, ntfy and webhooks. Nothing is preselected. The key is never stored, and Nexview only ever reads from Seerr.

sections.title: Accounts come along, ready to use
sections.where: Users step of the wizard
sections.body: One of Seerr's accounts becomes the owner, with a password you set in the wizard. For everyone else you tick who comes and pick a role per row; the default is user, and what the person was in Seerr stands next to it as a hint. Each account arrives with its display name, a username shaped from it, its count quota (Seerr's 0 means “no limit” and becomes exactly that), its personal region and language, its profile picture, and its Plex, Jellyfin or Emby identity. Plex people sign in through Plex as soon as the server is connected; everyone else sets a password via “Forgot password” or gets one from you.

sections.title: Everything in one go, or not at all
sections.where: Write step
sections.body: The wizard writes nothing until its last step. Then settings, block list, channels, owner and accounts land in a single transaction. If anything fails, the database stays empty and the wizard stays where it is; nothing is half done.

sections.title: The media server comes last
sections.where: Server step, after writing
sections.body: Plex through the usual code at plex.tv, with the server Seerr used marked in the list; Jellyfin and Emby through address and administrator sign-in, the address prefilled from Seerr. The step can be skipped. A report at the end says what was written, how each person gets in, which rows were left out and why, and what remains by hand.

small: The request history. What sits in Radarr and Sonarr, Nexview shows anyway; only who asked would carry over, and no storage is booked to anyone retroactively.
Passwords, watch lists, per-person notification addresses, Seerr's override rules and its discover sliders. None of them has a place in Nexview, and the wizard says so instead of pretending.
Seerr's own public address. It points at Seerr, not at Nexview.

0.29.1.lead: A maintenance release for the Seerr migration: the wizard now speaks the language you chose, all the way through. Before, the server built its hints in German and the English interface showed them unchanged.

sections.title: The migration wizard speaks your language
sections.where: On the very first start, path “From a running Seerr installation”
sections.body: The conversions on the account rows, the gaps per area, the labels of the preview, the reasons for rows left out and the list of what remains by hand in the report arrived as finished German sentences from the server. Now the server sends only an identifier and the numbers, and the interface builds the sentence in its own language. A test keeps both language files complete.

small: The wizard read a person's own region from Seerr under a wrong field name; it would have reached nobody. Measured against Seerr's source and fixed.

0.30.0.lead: Nexview connects to Home Assistant now, and everybody does it for themselves: enter your access key over there and you get your own figures and are notified about your own business. Along with a correction that was long overdue: storage sizes are finally called what they are.

sections.title: Home Assistant, for everybody in the house
sections.where: Profile → API tokens
sections.body:
Notification targets used to be an operator's business. An application that wanted to connect therefore needed an administrative key, and then received everything happening in the house instead of what concerned its owner.

Now the application registers itself, with the key it already has. It receives exactly what its owner also sees in their notification bell: their requests, their tickets, their storage. Anybody in the same household running their own Home Assistant gets their own, and neither sees the other's.

Your access keys then show where Nexview notifies, with a button to disconnect. A key marked *read only* may do this too, otherwise notifications would be the one reason to reach for the more powerful key.

sections.title: Where Nexview notifies
sections.where: Settings → Notifications, at the bottom
sections.body:
A list of every application that registered: who is being notified, through which key, at which address, and whether anything failed recently. Whoever runs a server should be able to see where it sends data.

Nothing is set up here, because the application does that itself. Disconnecting works.

sections.title: GiB now says GiB
sections.where: Everywhere a size appears
sections.body:
Nexview has always divided storage sizes by 1024³ and written "GB" next to them. That is the unit which divides by 1000³, and the difference is seven per cent. It showed up when comparing with Home Assistant: the same usage read as 100.3 GB there and 93 GB here. Both figures were right, only one of the two labels.

The name changed, not the arithmetic. Anybody who entered 300 still has exactly the same space as before, it now says "300 GiB". The other way round would have taken seven per cent off everyone's allowance without anybody touching a setting.

sections.title: House stock is shown separately
sections.where: Home page, "Library" tile
sections.body: "Used" threw together two very different things: what the residents requested, and what was here before Nexview or got taken over later. Only the first half counts against allowances and grows when somebody requests something. Both figures are there now.

small: `GET /api/v1/me` tells an integration who is knocking and what this key may do, as stable identifiers, not as a role. An administrator with a read-only token may approve nothing, and building against the role builds a button that always fails.

`GET /api/v1/storage/me` now also says whether the account gets anything attributed to it at all. For an administrator it does not: what they fetch belongs to the house. Their figures sit at zero, and that is a booking rather than a measurement.
The statistics carry the last sign-in per account, so "which accounts are asleep" can be answered without opening the user list, which drags mail addresses and avatars along.
A webhook payload carries its confirmation code in a field of its own. A machine no longer has to pick it out of a translated sentence.

0.30.1.lead: A hotfix for the Jellyfin sync, from a report with logs and measurements: seventeen minutes become about half a minute, a slow query no longer takes the library with it, and two syncs no longer run side by side.

sections.title: The Jellyfin sync no longer takes seventeen minutes
sections.where: Settings, Services, Media server, the Jellyfin tile, “Sync now”
sections.body: Nexview asks Jellyfin which titles each account has played. Jellyfin 10.11 answers that at a fixed price per request, no matter how small the page, and on one reporter's server the price was 53 seconds. Nexview asked for 19 pages. It now asks once per account, without the total count and without image data, and waits up to three minutes: about 25 seconds on that server instead of 17 minutes.

sections.title: A slow played-titles query no longer takes the library with it
sections.where: Same tile, the card with the title count
sections.body: When that one query timed out, the whole library read was discarded and the card said “Not synced yet” for weeks, although movies and series arrived in three seconds. The library is now read regardless. Series keep their watched flag from the previous run instead of losing it, and the log names the query that gave up.

sections.title: “Sync now” waits for a sync that is already running
sections.where: Same button
sections.body: Pressing it during the hourly sync used to start a second, identical one: the same questions to the same server twice, and two runs writing the same rows. The button now waits for the running sync and shows its result, including the error if that run failed for this server.

small: Emby shares the adapter and gets the same three changes. It never showed the problem, because it answers the played query in milliseconds. Plex is not affected.

0.31.0.lead: Nexview now reaches you while it is closed: every account can subscribe its own devices for web push, phone, tablet or computer. The same switches as for e-mail decide what arrives there.

sections.title: Web push for your own devices
sections.where: Profile, Notifications, tab “Web Push”
sections.body: One click on “Allow notifications”, and this browser gets notified even while Nexview is not open: the title is ready, the request is decided, a child wishes for something. Every device subscribes once and then appears in a list with its last delivery. A test message tells you right away whether anything arrives. Messages are encrypted end to end and signed with a key Nexview generates once; the browser’s push service only sees that something arrives.

sections.title: The same switches as for e-mail
sections.where: Same tab, right column
sections.body: What you get notified about belongs to your account, so it is the same on every device. The first device turns all switches on so the subscription does not run into a void; after that you turn off what you do not want. The monthly clean-up report stays an e-mail.

sections.title: On iPhone via the Home Screen
sections.where: Safari, share menu, “Add to Home Screen”
sections.body: Apple delivers web push only to pages that live on the Home Screen. Nexview now ships a manifest and icons for that and can sit on a Home Screen like an app, on Android and on a computer too. The page says on every device what is still missing: the Home Screen, the permission or https.

sections.title: Operators see where Nexview sends
sections.where: Settings, Channels, section “Callbacks”
sections.body: Subscribed devices appear next to the Home Assistant callbacks: whose they are, which browser, which push service. The subscription address itself is never shown; it is a key to the device. A row can be disconnected there.

small: Web push needs https. On a plain http address in the home network the page explains that instead of showing a dead button.
A device you remove is not silently subscribed again on the next visit, even though the browser would still allow it.
A subscription the push service no longer knows is dropped by Nexview on its own. A rejected signature is reported, not dropped.
